
`ariadne` integrates diverse biological resources spanning multiple omics
modalities, making it applicable to various omics data science scenarios focused
on enriching analyses with curated knowledge from public databases. This
tutorial demonstrates the following core applications of `ariadne`:

| **Use case** | **Resources** | **Objective** |
|--------------|---------------|---------------|
| Functional annotation | ChocoPhlAn, WoL | Annotate microbial or gene features (UniRef) with sequence-based related functional information (e.g., KO, EC, and Pfam) |
| Taxonomic translation | OTT, UniProt | Convert taxonomic names and ids across taxonomies (NCBI, SILVA, OTT, etc.) |
| Set enrichment analysis | BugSigDB, GM, GO, MSigDB | Test for enriched or depleted functional sets of features between conditions |
| Pathway enrichment analysis | KEGG, Rhea, WoL | Test for enriched or depleted metabolic pathways linked to features between conditions |
| Knowledge-driven association analysis | KEGG, UniProt | Test previously reported associations between different omics layers (e.g., microbes, metabolites and genes) |

First, we load `ariadne` and additional libraries used across this tutorial.

```{r lib, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ariadne)
library(anansi)
library(curatedMetagenomicData)
library(mia)
library(miaViz)
library(stringr)
library(DT)
```

We also import the `ariadne` resource graph that will be used to link resources
throughout this tutorial.

```{r}
# Import resource graph
graph <- ariadne()
```

# Functional annotation

Resources such as ChocoPhlAn and Web of Life (WoL) have been developed to
annotate microbial features and gene families with relevant functional
information, including KEGG Orthogroups (KOs), Pfam domains, enzyme commission
(EC) numbers and Gene Ontology (GO). This allows to derive actionable insight
directly from biological assays.

Resources such as ChocoPhlAn and the Web of Life (WoL) annotate microbial
features and gene families with functional metadata—such as KEGG Orthogroups
(KOs), Pfam domains, Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers and Gene Ontology (GO)
terms—enabling the derivation of biological insights directly from omics
datasets.

We import and process the Castro-NallarE_2015 dataset from
[curatedMetagenomicData](https://doi.org/10.18129/B9.bioc.curatedMetagenomicData),
which entails 32 oral cavity microbiome samples from individuals with Chron's
Disease, Type-2 Diabetes and schizophrenia.

We import and preprocess the `Castro-NallarE_2015` dataset from
[curatedMetagenomicData](https://doi.org/10.18129/B9.bioc.curatedMetagenomicData), comprising 32 oral cavity microbiome samples from individuals with Crohn's
disease, Type 2 diabetes and schizophrenia.

```{r}
# Load gene family experiment
genes <- curatedMetagenomicData(
    "Castro-NallarE_2015.gene_families", dryrun = FALSE
)

# Extract experiment from list
genes <- genes[[1]]

# Keep only unstratified gene families
genes <- genes[str_detect(rownames(genes), fixed("|"), negate = TRUE), ]

# View experiment
genes
```

We query the three shortest paths connecting UniRef90 gene families to Gut
Metabolic Modules (GMMs), selecting the primary path mediated by ChocoPhlAn.

```{r}
# Search first three paths
searchPath(graph, uniref90 ~ gmm, k = 3)
```

For users familiar with the bioBakery suite, this operation corresponds to
`humann_regroup_table` from [HUMAnN](https://github.com/biobakery/humann).
However, ariadne seamlessly concatenates preliminary and successive mapping
steps to directly link distinct feature spaces (e.g., microbes $\rightarrow$
UniRef $\rightarrow$ KOs $\rightarrow$ modules).

```{r}
# Weave bindings between taxa and GMMs
uniref2gmm <- weaveComplex(graph, uniref90 ~ gmm, init = rownames(genes))

# View linkmap
datatable(uniref2gmm)
```

Alternatively, WoL can be utilized. Because UniRef-to-KO bindings are exclusive
to earlier releases, we explicitly import a previous version of the resource
graph.

```{r}
# Import past release of the resource graph
graph <- ariadne(versions = list(WoL = "v20April2021"))

# Weave path through WoL
uniref2gmm <- weaveComplex(
    graph,
    uniref90 ~ gmm,
    init = rownames(genes),
    res.name = c("WoL", "GM")
)
```

Next, we incorporate these mappings into the experiment object and agglomerate
the features by module.


```{r}
# Add modules to experiment side information
genes <- addModules(genes, uniref2gmm, as = "names")

# Agglomerate experiment by modules
mod.se <- agglomerateByModule(
    genes, by = "rows", group = levels(uniref2gmm$gmm.name)
)

# View experiment object
mod.se
```

Finally, per-sample module abundances are visualised using a heatmap.

```{r}
# Visualise per-sample module abundances
plotHeatmap(mod.se, assay.type = "gene_families")
```

# Taxonomic translation

Taxonomic harmonization and cross-referencing across nomenclature systems are
frequent bottlenecks in integrative multi-omics analyses. ariadne facilitates
robust ID translation and name resolution across diverse taxonomies (e.g., NCBI,
SILVA, OTT and Greengenes).

First, we load the built-in butyrate linkmap containing microbial features
associated with butyrate biosynthesis.

```{r}
# Import butyrate linkmap
data("butyrate", package = "ariadne")

# View butyrate linkmap
datatable(butyrate)
```

We map NCBI taxon identifiers to their corresponding binomial names.

```{r}
# Link taxon ids to names
tax2name <- linkNames(graph, "taxid", ids = butyrate$taxid)

# View linkmap
datatable(tax2name)
```

Conversely, NCBI taxon IDs can be retrieved from taxon names, which need to be
exact.

```{r}
# Link taxon names to ids
name2tax <- linkNames(graph, "taxid", names = butyrate$taxid.name)

# View linkmap
datatable(name2tax)
```

Alternatively, we can query the Open Tree of Life Taxonomy (OTT) to resolve
taxon names using approximate string matching, accommodating partial or
imprecise entries.

```{r}
# Link taxon names to OTT ids
name2ott <- linkNames(graph, "ott", names = butyrate$taxid.name)

# Map OTT ids to NCBI taxon ids
name2tax <- weavePath(graph, ott.name ~ taxid, init = rev(name2ott))

# View linkmap
datatable(name2tax)
```

OTT also bridges disparate taxonomies. Here, we translate NCBI taxon IDs from
the butyrate linkmap to corresponding SILVA SSU identifiers.

```{r}
# Convert taxid to silva
tax2silva <- weavePath(
    graph,
    taxid ~ silva_ssu,
    init = butyrate$taxid,
    use.names = FALSE
)

# View linkmap
datatable(tax2silva)
```

Similarly, WoL enables the translation of Greengenes identifiers to NCBI taxon
IDs.

```{r}
# Convert greengenes to taxid
gg2tax <- weavePath(graph, greengenes ~ taxid)

# View linkmap
datatable(gg2tax)
```

# Set enrichment analysis

Leveraging prior functional or phenotypic annotations, set enrichment analysis
tests whether predefined feature sets (genes, taxa, or metabolites) are over-
or under-represented. Common repositories include GO or MSigDB for genes and
BugSigDB for microbial signatures.

Feature sets of interest can be queried via keyword matching against descriptive
names. For instance, we extract attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
(ADHD)-related microbial signatures from BugSigDB via the ariadne graph.

```{r}
# Retrieve all unique BugSig sets
bugsig2name <- linkNames(graph, "bugsig")

# Extract sets related to ADHD
adhd.sets <- bugsig2name[str_detect(bugsig2name$bugsig.name, fixed("ADHD")), ]

# View sets of interest
datatable(adhd.sets)
```

We load and preprocess the
[Tengeler2020](https://microbiome.github.io/mia/reference/Tengeler2020.html)
dataset, comprising stool metagenomic and metabolomic profiles from humanised
ADHD mice.

```{r}
# Import experiment object
data("Tengeler2020", package = "mia")

# Rename experiment object
tse <- Tengeler2020

# Transform counts to relative abundance
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "relabundance")

# View experiment object
tse
```

We map microbial features at the genus level to their corresponding OTT taxon
IDs to establish initial values for graph traversal.


```{r}
# Link taxon names to OTT ids
name2tax <- linkNames(graph, "ott", names = rowData(tse)$Genus)

# View linkmap
datatable(name2tax)
```
We weave a path from OTT taxon names to BugSig sets via OTT IDs, yielding a
linkmap directly compatible with our experiment object.

```{r}
# Weave path from taxname to bugsig
tax2bugsig <- weavePath(graph, ott.name ~ bugsig, init = rev(name2tax))

# View linkmap
datatable(tax2bugsig)
```

This can be added to the experiment object and used to agglomerate the assay
by set, which returns the per-sample abundance for each set.

```{r warning = FALSE}
# Add modules information to experiment
tse <- addModules(tse, tax2bugsig, key = "Genus", as = "names")

# Limit sets to those found by weave (add support to agglomerateByModule)
adhd.sets <- adhd.sets[adhd.sets$bugsig %in% levels(tax2bugsig$bugsig), ]

# Agglomerate experiment by module
adhd.se <- agglomerateByModule(tse, by = "rows", group = adhd.sets$bugsig.name)

# View results
adhd.se
```

Finally, we visualise per-sample set abundances using a heatmap.

```{r}
# Visualise per-sample module abundance
plotHeatmap(adhd.se, assay.type = "relabundance", col.var = "patient_status")
```

# Pathway enrichment analysis

Analogous to set enrichment, pathway enrichment analysis tests for enriched or
depleted metabolic pathways based on feature coverage. Representative resources
include KEGG and MetaCyc for comprehensive microbial metabolism, alongside specialised databases like enviPath for xenobiotic biotransformation.

KEGG pathways can be mapped from KOs or ECs, ideally via KEGG reactions.

```{r}
# Search paths from ec to kegg pathways
searchPath(graph, ec ~ kegg_path, include = "kegg_rxn", k = 3)
```

We link EC numbers to KEGG pathways while specifying a custom coverage
threshold.

```{r}
# Weave path from ec to kegg pathways
ec2path <- weaveComplex(
    graph,
    ec ~ kegg_path,
    include = "kegg_rxn",
    threshold = 0.5
)

# View linkmap
datatable(ec2path)
```

The MetaCyc pathways are provided by WoL2. However, they correspond to
an earlier version of MetaCyc before it became commercially available.

```{r}
# Search paths from ec to metacyc pathways
searchPath(graph, ec ~ metacyc_path, k = 3)
```

Similarly, EC numbers are linked to associated MetaCyc pathways while also
estimating pathway coverage by feature.

```{r}
# Weave path from ec to metacyc pathways
ec2path <- weaveComplex(graph, ec ~ metacyc_path)

# View linkmap
datatable(ec2path)
```

# Knowledge-driven association analysis

[anansi](https://doi.org/10.18129/B9.bioc.anansi) evaluates pairwise
associations between dual-omics modalities (e.g., microbiome and metabolome)
within a unified experiment, restricting statistical comparisons to prior
biologically relevant or documented interactions. ariadne supplies the necessary
relational mappings to constrain this search space.

We load the
[HintikkaXOData](https://microbiome.github.io/mia/reference/HintikkaXOData.html)
dataset, including stool metabolomic and metagenomic profiles from mice
subjected to low and high-fat dietary regimes.

```{r}
# Import dataset
data("HintikkaXOData", package = "mia")

# Rename object
mae <- HintikkaXOData

# View multi-assay experiment
mae
```

We agglomerate the microbiome experiment by Genus and sanitise feature names
to maximise their successful conversion to OTT taxon ids.

```{r}
# Agglomerate microbiome experiment by Genus
mae[["microbiota"]] <- agglomerateByRank(mae[["microbiota"]], rank = "Genus")

# Remove rank prefix from taxon names
rownames(mae[["microbiota"]]) <- mae[["microbiota"]] |>
    rownames() |>
    str_remove(fixed("D_5__"))

# Link taxon names to OTT ids
name2tax <- linkNames(graph, "ott", names = rownames(mae[["microbiota"]]))

# View linkmap
datatable(name2tax)
```

We map metabolite identifiers to corresponding KEGG compound IDs. In practice,
unmatched entries typically require manual curation.

```{r}
# Link metabolite names to KEGG compound ids
name2cpd <- linkNames(graph, "kegg_cpd", names = rownames(mae[["metabolites"]]))

# View linkmap
datatable(name2cpd)
```

We then weave the path linking taxon names to KEGG compound IDs.

```{r}
# Weave path from taxon names to KEGG compound ids
tax2cpd <- weavePath(
    graph,
    ott.name ~ kegg_cpd,
    init = rev(name2tax),
    res.name = c("WoL", "KEGG")
)

# Remove KEGG compound id column
tax2cpd$kegg_cpd <- NULL

# Rename linkmap variables
names(tax2cpd) <- c("microbiota", "metabolites")

# View linkmap
datatable(tax2cpd)
```

Finally, we construct an anansi Web object and execute the association analysis.

```{r}
# Create anansi web object
web <- weaveWeb(mae, microbiota ~ metabolites, link = tax2cpd)

# Perform association analysis
out <- anansi(web)
```

Resulting associations are visualised via a forest plot.

```{r}
# Visualise associations
plotAnansi(out)
```
